name: Tuxedo / dinner suit

card.summary: A formal evening suit with satin or grosgrain lapels, braided trousers and a bow tie, worn to make the wearer look sharp and polished at black-tie events.
card.aka: tux, dinner jacket, DJ, black tie, smoking

quick.overview:
The tuxedo, called a dinner suit or dinner jacket in British usage, is the standard dress for black-tie evening events. It is typically a black or midnight-blue jacket with silk facings on the lapels, matching trousers with a side braid, a white dress shirt and a black bow tie.

Its appearance payoff is a clean, high-contrast silhouette: the dark jacket against a white shirt draws attention to the face, and a close tailored fit shapes the shoulders and waist. Fit and formality conventions are the main points of discussion among style communities.
quick.how: People wear it for weddings, galas and evening events with a dress code of black tie, either rented or owned and tailored. Traditional components include a low waistcoat or cummerbund (not both), a turndown-collar shirt, studs and cufflinks, and patent leather or plain Oxford shoes.
quick.risks: The main risks are cost and fit: an ill-fitting or rented tuxedo reads differently from a tailored one. Traditional conventions vary by region and occasion, and style guides differ on details such as wing collars and lapel type.

lead: A tuxedo (American English) or dinner suit (British English) is the formal evening suit worn for black-tie occasions. The jacket is traditionally black or midnight blue, usually single-breasted with one button, with lapels faced in silk satin or grosgrain, worn with matching trousers, a white shirt and a black bow tie.[2] People wear it because the high-contrast formula of dark cloth against a white shirt gives a clean, polished silhouette, and because tailoring the shoulders, waist and trouser break makes the wearer look sharper at weddings, galas and dinners.

Black tie is classed as a semi-formal, or half-dress, code: below white tie and above business dress.[2][7] It is traditionally worn after 6 p.m. or after sundown in winter.[2] The suit is known as a dinner jacket or dinner suit (often DJ) in Britain, a tuxedo or tux in the US, and a smoking in many European languages, after the 19th-century smoking jacket.[1][2]

The garment dates from the 1860s, when the Prince of Wales ordered a tailless evening jacket from the Savile Row tailors Henry Poole & Co., and it took its American name from Tuxedo Park, New York, in the 1880s.[2][4][5] Since the 1960s it has also been adapted for women, most famously in Yves Saint Laurent's 1966 Le Smoking.[3]

paras: The traditional jacket is wool, mohair or a blend in black or midnight blue, single-breasted with one button and jetted pockets. Lapels are peak or shawl, faced in satin or grosgrain; notch lapels are regarded as less formal. Vents are absent on the most formal jackets, with side vents next and a centre vent the least formal.[2]

Trousers carry no turn-ups or belt loops and have a single braid down each outer seam matching the lapel facing; they are worn with braces. The waist is covered by a low-cut waistcoat or a cummerbund, never both, with the cummerbund's pleats facing upward. The shirt is white with a marcella or pleated bib, a turndown collar and double (French) cuffs, and the bow tie is black, self-tied and matches the facings.[2]

Details include studs and cufflinks (onyx or mother-of-pearl are typical), black silk or fine-wool socks, and shoes in patent leather court shoes or plain-toe Oxfords; brogued or open-laced Derby shoes are generally considered too informal. A white pocket square and a boutonniere such as a carnation are traditional accessories, and visible wristwatches are traditionally avoided in favour of pocket watches.[2]

Because the jacket is cut close, ventless or lightly vented, and covered at the waist by a waistcoat or cummerbund, the outfit emphasises a defined shoulder and waist line and a long uninterrupted leg line from the single trouser braid.[2] The white shirt bib frames the face against black or midnight-blue cloth. Style communities and tailors commonly describe getting the jacket's shoulders, sleeve length and trouser break tailored as the main way to improve how a tuxedo looks, compared with an off-the-rack or rented one.
Midnight blue rivalled black by the mid-1930s and has become popular again in the 21st century; guides often note that in artificial light it can read as a deeper black.[2]

In the formality conventions described by Wikipedia, black tie is traditionally worn after 6 p.m., shawl and peak lapels are more formal than notch, ventless jackets are the most formal, and patent leather is more formal than matte leather.[2] A wing collar is contested: many authorities reserve it for white tie, though attached wing collars have been popular with American men since the 1980s.[2]

Warm-climate variants include the ivory white dinner jacket, which has self-faced lapels and is usually worn with a turndown collar and cummerbund; British convention long held it appropriate only abroad. Some invitations specify the Red Sea rig, with the jacket removed in heat, in certain expatriate communities.[2] Muted red accents such as maroon cummerbunds are traditional, while the bow tie stays black.[2]

White tie, with a tailcoat, white waistcoat and white bow tie, is the more formal code and is now reserved for the most ceremonial events such as state dinners and some balls; the Met Gala used white-tie dress codes in 2014 and 2022.[6] In the standard ladder of dress codes, black tie is the semi-formal tier, followed by informal dress such as suits and cocktail dresses.[7]

The earliest recorded tailless evening jacket is a midnight-blue silk smoking jacket ordered by the Prince of Wales, later Edward VII, from Henry Poole & Co. on Savile Row, for use at Sandringham; Wikipedia's article on the firm dates it to 1860, while the black tie article gives 1865.[2][4] The jacket was first thought informal and associated with warm-weather settings such as Cowes.[2]

The American name comes from Tuxedo Park, a gated community developed from 1885 by Pierre Lorillard IV, with a clubhouse built in 1886.[5] According to the village's article, James Brown Potter brought the garment there after being introduced to it by the Prince of Wales; another account credits Griswold Lorillard, who with friends wore a tailless coat at the October 1886 autumn ball, though that account may refer to a mess jacket.[2][4][5] "Dinner jacket" appears in British menswear around 1887 and "tuxedo" in American usage around 1888.[2]

In the Edwardian era black waistcoats and bow ties became the convention. After World War I the dinner jacket became established semi-formal evening wear, and double-breasted styles, turndown collars and cummerbunds grew popular in the interwar years. The 1950s to 1970s brought colour, pattern, ruffled shirts and wider lapels, mass-market retailers began offering coloured suits to rental customers in the 1970s, and black returned in the 1980s and 90s with notch lapels and business-suit details such as flap pockets and centre vents.[2]

Women's black tie has traditionally been an ankle- or tea-length gown, though today it spans from near-white-tie formality to a little black dress, and palazzo-cut evening trousers are accepted in England.[2] In 1966 Yves Saint Laurent introduced Le Smoking, a women's dinner suit with a more feminine collar, narrowed waist and trousers cut to lengthen the leg. Wikipedia credits it with helping establish the women's power suit and pantsuit; model Danielle Luquet de Saint Germain and singer Francoise Hardy are named among those associated with it.[3] Princess Diana later wore men's black-tie accessories in public.[2]

Black tie is worn at private and public dinners, balls, galas, proms and cruise-ship formal nights. Cunard relaxed its standards in 2013 and by 2015 accepted a dinner jacket, dark suit, national dress or military uniform. Glyndebourne still requires black tie, and some British debating societies, including the Oxford Union and Durham Union, hold debates in it, while the Cambridge Union abolished its requirement in 2002.[1][2]

At US weddings black tie is common in place of morning dress, though etiquette authorities regard it before 6 p.m. as unusual and in the UK and Europe it is seldom worn at church ceremonies. Boys generally do not wear dinner jackets before about 15.[2] Slang includes "monkey suit" and, since 1918, "soup and fish."[2]

timeline.event: The Prince of Wales orders a midnight-blue silk smoking jacket from Henry Poole & Co. (dated 1860 or 1865 depending on source).[2][4]
Pierre Lorillard IV begins developing Tuxedo Park, New York.[5]
Tuxedo Club's autumn ball; Griswold Lorillard and friends reportedly wear tailless coats, and James Brown Potter wears a Poole jacket at the club.[2][4][5]
The term dinner jacket appears in British menswear.[2]
The term tuxedo appears in American usage and polite society accepts the jacket for informal evening wear.[2]
The nickname soup and fish is first recorded.[2]
Midnight blue rivals black; cummerbunds and turndown collars spread.[2]
Yves Saint Laurent introduces Le Smoking, a women's dinner suit.[3]
Mass-market retailers begin renting coloured and white full suits.[2]
Black returns as the norm; notch lapels and attached wing collars become common in the US.[2]
The Cambridge Union abolishes mandatory black tie for debates.[2]
Cunard accepts a dinner jacket, dark suit, national dress or uniform on formal nights.[2]

lore.intro: Style communities debate black-tie conventions, usually in terms of what reads as correct and what flatters.

claims.believers: Traditionalists hold that the jacket should be black or midnight blue, with midnight blue looking richer under evening light.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes midnight blue rivalled black by the mid-1930s and is popular again, while colour and pattern appeared in the 1950s to 1970s.[2]

claims.claim: Never wear a waistcoat and cummerbund together
claims.believers: Style guides state the waist is covered by one or the other.[2]
claims.experts: The black tie convention described in reference works is a low waistcoat or a cummerbund, never both.[2]

claims.claim: Peak and shawl lapels are more formal than notch
claims.believers: Many guides rank peak and shawl lapels above notch.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that notch lapels are considered less formal and returned for good in the 1980s.[2]

claims.claim: Wing collars belong with white tie only
claims.believers: Purists reserve the wing collar for white tie.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes the question is contested and attached wing collars have been popular with American men since the 1980s.[2]

claims.claim: Wear black tie only after 6 p.m.
claims.experts: Etiquette authorities still see daytime black tie as unusual, though it is common at US weddings.[2]

claims.believers: Traditional guidance favours a pocket watch.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia records this as a traditional convention.[2]

claims.claim: The tuxedo originated with a Tuxedo Park ball
claims.believers: A popular account credits Griswold Lorillard at the 1886 autumn ball.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says details are unclear and the village article suggests that account may refer to a mess jacket, with Potter and the Prince of Wales also credited.[2][4][5]
